meta.title: Simple Machines: Six Ways to Win at Physics
meta.topic: The 6 simple machines (lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw)

plan.title: Simple Machines: Six Ways to Win at Physics
plan.hook: Six ancient inventions, one shared bargain: give up distance, gain force. Every machine in this course is that trade wearing a different shape.
objectives: For each of the six simple machines, state what it trades and what it gains
Compute a lever's ideal mechanical advantage from its arm lengths
Explain how a movable pulley halves ideal effort and what it costs in rope
Recognise the inclined plane hiding inside both the wedge and the screw
prerequisites: Middle-school ideas of force and distance

sections.heading: Lever
points: A lever trades force and distance about a fulcrum
Ideal mechanical advantage is effort arm over load arm
Effort and load move on opposite sides of the fixed fulcrum — the diagram shows a 3:1 arm ratio

sections.heading: Wheel and axle
points: A larger wheel turns a smaller axle
The assembly rotates together about the same centre, at the same angular speed
Force advantage is proportional to the radius ratio — same rotation, different rim force

sections.heading: Pulley
points: A movable pulley can halve the effort for ideal frictionless rope
The cost is rope length: the load rises half as far as the rope you pull
The simple setup in the diagram is a 2:1 arrangement

sections.heading: Inclined plane
points: A gentler ramp reduces the required force
The trade is distance: the same height gain takes a longer path
Steep versus gentle ramps reach the same height with different force and distance

sections.heading: Wedge
points: A wedge converts an input force into sideways splitting forces
The force enters along the drive direction and exits sideways along the faces
Driving the wedge pushes the material apart on both sides

sections.heading: Screw
points: A screw is a helical inclined plane — a ramp wrapped into a helix
One full turn advances the screw by exactly one pitch
The handle sweeps a full circle for that single pitch of advance — the same force-for-distance trade

sections.heading: Lever
sections.body: A lever trades force and distance about a fulcrum. Ideal mechanical advantage is effort arm over load arm.
sections.visual: Effort and load move opposite the fulcrum. Scrub to see the 3:1 arm ratio in motion.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Lever"><title>Lever</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Lever · effort vs load</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><line class="lw-lever-bar" x1="150" y1="220" x2="650" y2="220" stroke="#7cc7ff" stroke-width="6"/><circle cx="400" cy="220" r="10" fill="#ffd479"/><circle class="lw-lever-effort" cx="180" cy="220" r="14" fill="#7ee2a8"/><circle class="lw-lever-load" cx="580" cy="220" r="18" fill="#b39dff"/><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Ideal · fulcrum fixed</text></svg>

questions.q: What does a lever trade, and around what?
questions.hint: Two quantities are exchanged, pivoting on a fixed point.
questions.answer: A lever trades force and distance about a fulcrum. A longer effort arm means less force needed, paid for with more movement on the effort side.

questions.q: How is a lever's ideal mechanical advantage computed?
questions.hint: It is a ratio of the two arms.
questions.answer: Effort arm divided by load arm. The diagram's 3:1 arm ratio gives an ideal mechanical advantage of 3.

sections.heading: Wheel and axle
sections.body: A larger wheel turns a smaller axle with a force advantage proportional to the radius ratio.
sections.visual: Wheel and axle rotate together about the same center.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Wheel and axle"><title>Wheel and axle</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Wheel and axle</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><circle class="lw-rotate" cx="400" cy="210" r="90" fill="none" stroke="#7cc7ff" stroke-width="4"/><circle class="lw-rotate" cx="400" cy="210" r="30" fill="#172331" stroke="#ffd479" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Same angular speed · different rim force</text></svg>

questions.q: Why does turning the big wheel give a force advantage at the axle?
questions.hint: Both parts share one rotation but have different radii.
questions.answer: The wheel and axle rotate together about the same centre, so they share angular speed, but the larger radius converts the turn into a force advantage proportional to the radius ratio.

questions.q: Do the wheel and axle turn at different speeds?
questions.hint: The diagram is explicit about what they share.
questions.answer: No — they rotate together at the same angular speed. What differs is the rim force, thanks to the different radii.

sections.heading: Pulley
sections.body: A movable pulley can halve the effort for ideal frictionless rope, at the cost of more rope length.
sections.visual: Pull the free end; the load rises half as far as the rope you pull in a simple 2:1 setup.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Pulley"><title>Pulley</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Pulley · 2:1 ideal</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><circle class="lw-pulley-wheel" cx="400" cy="120" r="28" fill="none" stroke="#7cc7ff" stroke-width="4"/><path class="lw-pulley-rope" d="M400 148 L400 260" stroke="#9aa6b8" stroke-width="3"/><rect class="lw-pulley-load" x="375" y="260" width="50" height="40" fill="#b39dff"/><path class="lw-pulley-pull" d="M372 120 L280 200" stroke="#ffd479" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Ideal rope · no friction</text></svg>

questions.q: What does a movable pulley give you, and what does it charge?
questions.hint: The gain is in effort; the price is measured in rope.
questions.answer: It can halve the effort for ideal frictionless rope — and the cost is rope length: in the simple 2:1 setup the load rises half as far as the rope you pull.

questions.q: You pull 2 metres of rope in the diagram's 2:1 setup. How far does the load rise?
questions.hint: Apply the ratio in the diagram's caption.
questions.answer: One metre. The load rises half as far as the rope you pull in a simple 2:1 setup.

sections.heading: Inclined plane
sections.body: A gentler ramp reduces required force but increases distance for the same height gain.
sections.visual: Compare steep and gentle ramps: blocks climb as force arrows show the tradeoff.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Inclined plane"><title>Inclined plane</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Gentle vs steep ramp</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M60 300 L280 140 L280 300 Z" fill="#172331" stroke="#7cc7ff"/><path d="M420 300 L720 140 L720 300 Z" fill="#172331" stroke="#7ee2a8"/><rect class="lw-ramp-block-steep" x="70" y="250" width="36" height="24" fill="#ffd479"/><rect class="lw-ramp-block-gentle" x="400" y="265" width="36" height="24" fill="#ffd479"/><path class="lw-ramp-force-steep" d="M100 240 L140 200" stroke="#b39dff" stroke-width="3"/><path class="lw-ramp-force-gentle" d="M430 250 L500 220" stroke="#b39dff" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Same height · different force and distance</text></svg>

questions.q: What changes when a ramp is made gentler?
questions.hint: Force and distance move in opposite directions.
questions.answer: The required force drops, but the distance travelled for the same height gain increases. Gentler ramp: less force, more distance.

questions.q: Do a steep ramp and a gentle ramp deliver the same height gain?
questions.hint: The diagram compares them on exactly this point.
questions.answer: Yes — same height, different force and distance. The plane trades one against the other; it does not change the height.

sections.heading: Wedge
sections.body: A wedge converts an input force into sideways splitting forces along its faces.
sections.visual: Drive the wedge; side forces push material apart.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Wedge"><title>Wedge</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Wedge · split forces</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><path class="lw-wedge" d="M400 100 L460 280 L340 280 Z" fill="#172331" stroke="#7cc7ff" stroke-width="3"/><path class="lw-wedge-force" d="M400 90 L400 60" stroke="#ffd479" stroke-width="3"/><path class="lw-wedge-left" d="M350 200 L300 200" stroke="#7ee2a8" stroke-width="3"/><path class="lw-wedge-right" d="M450 200 L500 200" stroke="#7ee2a8" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Input down · outputs sideways</text></svg>

questions.q: What does a wedge do to the force you drive it with?
questions.hint: The output points in a different direction than the input.
questions.answer: It converts the input force into sideways splitting forces along its faces: input down, outputs sideways, pushing the material apart.

questions.q: Why does driving a wedge split material instead of just denting it?
questions.hint: Follow the direction of the forces along the faces.
questions.answer: Because the faces redirect the drive force sideways. Both sides of the material are pushed apart along the wedge's faces as it advances.

sections.heading: Screw
sections.body: A screw is a helical inclined plane. One turn advances the screw by one pitch.
sections.visual: The thread is a helical ramp. One full turn advances the screw by one pitch while the handle turns a full circle.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Screw"><title>Screw</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Screw · helix as ramp</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><rect class="lw-screw-body" x="360" y="100" width="80" height="200" rx="8" fill="#172331" stroke="#7cc7ff" stroke-width="3"/><path class="lw-screw-pitch" d="M360 140 Q400 160 440 140 T440 180 T440 220 T440 260" fill="none" stroke="#ffd479" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">One turn · one pitch of advance</text></svg>

questions.q: What is a screw, geometrically?
questions.hint: One of the other machines in this course, wrapped up.
questions.answer: A helical inclined plane — a ramp wound into a helix. The thread is a helical ramp.

questions.q: How far does a screw advance in one full turn?
questions.hint: The advance has its own name in the text.
questions.answer: Exactly one pitch. One turn of the handle — a full circle — advances the screw by a single pitch.

questions.q: A lever's effort arm is three times its load arm. Its ideal mechanical advantage is…
questions.explain: Ideal mechanical advantage is effort arm over load arm: 3 ÷ 1 = 3, the 3:1 arm ratio shown in the diagram.

questions.q: On a lever, the effort and load sit…
choices: On the same side of the fulcrum
On opposite sides of the fulcrum
questions.explain: The visual states it: effort and load move opposite the fulcrum — they act on opposite sides of the fixed pivot.

questions.q: The force advantage of a wheel and axle is proportional to…
questions.explain: A larger wheel turns a smaller axle with a force advantage proportional to the radius ratio — same angular speed, different rim force.

questions.q: Wheel and axle rotate…
choices: Together about the same centre at the same angular speed
Only when no load is attached
questions.explain: The diagram is explicit: wheel and axle rotate together about the same center, at the same angular speed; the rim forces differ because the radii differ.

questions.q: In the simple 2:1 pulley setup, halving the effort costs you…
choices: Twice the rope pulled for the same rise
questions.explain: The load rises half as far as the rope you pull, so raising it a given height takes twice that length of rope. The halved effort is for ideal frictionless rope.

questions.q: "Ideal" in this section's pulley assumes…
questions.explain: The text says the movable pulley can halve the effort for ideal frictionless rope — the idealisation is about friction, and the cost is rope length.

questions.q: Making a ramp gentler…
choices: Reduces required force but increases distance for the same height
Changes the height you can reach
questions.explain: A gentler ramp reduces required force but increases distance for the same height gain — steep and gentle ramps reach the same height with different force and distance.

questions.q: Two ramps reach the same platform, one steep and one gentle. Compared with the steep one, the gentle ramp needs…
choices: The same force over the same distance
questions.explain: That is the plane's bargain, stated in the body: gentler slope, smaller force, longer path, same height.

questions.q: A wedge converts an input force into…
choices: Sideways splitting forces along its faces
questions.explain: Drive the wedge and the side forces push material apart: input down, outputs sideways along the faces.

questions.q: The wedge is most closely related to which other machine in this course?
choices: The inclined plane — its faces are ramps
questions.explain: A wedge's faces are inclined planes: the drive force travels along the ramp-like faces and emerges sideways as splitting force.

questions.q: One full turn of a screw advances it by…
choices: One full thread length of the screw
It depends on the force applied
questions.explain: The body and diagram agree: one turn advances the screw by one pitch, while the handle turns a full circle.

questions.q: A screw is best described as…
choices: A lever wrapped in a coil
A wedge that rotates in place only
questions.explain: A screw is a helical inclined plane: the thread is a helical ramp, which is why turning trades a long circular path for a short advance.

sections.title: Trade force and distance about a fulcrum
bullets: A lever pivots on a fulcrum, effort on one side, load on the other.
Ideal mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm.
Longer effort arm: less force, more movement.
sections.notes: The lever is the template for every machine here: arrange the geometry so a small force moving far balances a large force moving little. The arm ratio is the whole story.
sections.visual: Effort and load move opposite the fulcrum. Scrub to see the 3:1 arm ratio in motion.

sections.title: One rotation, two radii
bullets: Wheel and axle rotate together about the same centre.
Same angular speed, different rim force.
Force advantage is proportional to the radius ratio.
sections.notes: Bolt a big wheel to a small axle and one turn serves both: your hands travel the wheel's long rim path while the axle winds with multiplied force.
sections.visual: Wheel and axle rotate together about the same center.

sections.title: Half the effort, twice the rope
bullets: A movable pulley can halve the effort (ideal, frictionless rope).
The load rises half as far as the rope you pull.
The diagram's setup is a simple 2:1.
sections.notes: The pulley bills you in rope. Halve the pull and you pay double the pull length — the same bargain as the lever, collected differently.
sections.visual: Pull the free end; the load rises half as far as the rope you pull in a simple 2:1 setup.

sections.title: Same height, gentler price
bullets: A ramp trades a steep lift for a longer, gentler climb.
Gentler ramp: less force, more distance.
sections.notes: Nobody lifts a piano straight up a wall when a ramp exists. The plane spreads the same height over more distance so the force at any moment stays manageable.
sections.visual: Compare steep and gentle ramps: blocks climb as force arrows show the tradeoff.

sections.title: Force in, split sideways
bullets: Drive force enters along the wedge.
The faces redirect it into sideways splitting forces.
Material is pushed apart on both sides.
sections.notes: A wedge is two ramps back to back. The blow travels down; the faces translate it into an outward push that tears the material's seam open.
sections.visual: Drive the wedge; side forces push material apart.

sections.title: A ramp wound into a helix
bullets: A screw is a helical inclined plane.
One full turn advances the screw by one pitch.
The handle sweeps a full circle for that single pitch of advance.
sections.notes: Unwrap a screw's thread and you find the inclined plane again, coiled. Turning trades a long circular sweep for a tiny, forceful advance — one pitch per turn.
sections.visual: The thread is a helical ramp. One full turn advances the screw by one pitch while the handle turns a full circle.

enrichment.audioTitle: Simple Machines: Six Ways to Win at Physics — a conversation

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Six machines, one bargain. Start with the lever: what is being traded, and around what point?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Force and distance, traded about the fulcrum.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: And the ideal mechanical advantage if the effort arm is three times the load arm?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Effort arm over load arm — three.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Good. Wheel and axle: the wheel turns the axle. Do they spin at different speeds?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: No — together, same centre, same angular speed. The force advantage comes from the radius ratio: different rim force.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Pulley next. A movable pulley halves your effort. What is the catch?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Rope. The load rises half as far as the rope pulled, so you haul twice the length — and that is for ideal frictionless rope.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Inclined plane: two ramps to the same platform, one steep, one gentle. Compare them.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Same height either way. The gentle one needs less force but over more distance.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Now the wedge — where does the force come out?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Sideways. You drive it down and its faces push the material apart.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Last one. What is a screw, really?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: An inclined plane wrapped into a helix. One full turn advances it by exactly one pitch.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Which makes all six the same trade in six costumes: distance surrendered, force gained. If you can say what each one charges, you understand all of them.
